Remonstrate

rih-MON-strayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To remonstrate is to say or plead in protest; to argue forcefully against something.

Neighbors gathered outside city hall to remonstrate against the proposed highway that would cut straight through the old park.

Worked Example

Rather than simply refusing the assignment, the intern chose to remonstrate with her supervisor, calmly explaining why the deadline was impossible to meet.

To remonstrate is to voice strong disagreement or protest, usually while still trying to be heard and reasoned with.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

protest: to express strong disagreement or objection

object: to express opposition to something

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

comply: to go along with a rule or request without objection

acquiesce: to accept something without protest

Where it sits · how forceful the objection becomes — grumble → remonstrate → revolt

grumble vs. remonstrate: To grumble is a mild, informal way of complaining, much quieter than an organized protest.

revolt vs. remonstrate: A revolt is an organized, sometimes violent uprising against authority -- a far more extreme form of resistance.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — re-

prefix — re-: back, intensively (Latin)

root — monstr(are)

root — monstr(are): to show, to point out (Latin)

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin re- plus monstrare ('to show') plus the verb suffix -ate: literally 'to show back.' To remonstrate is to show someone your strong disagreement -- pleading or arguing against something out loud.

Use the root in a new word: demonstrate

Use the root in a new word: demonstrate: The scientist wanted to demonstrate her theory using a simple classroom experiment.

Root Check

Word Choice

Remonstrate is a formal word -- you'll usually see it describing organized protest (to a board, a council, an official) rather than an ordinary personal argument.
